people.name: St Bernadette Soubirous
people.bio: Born at Lourdes, the eldest child of a ruined miller, Bernadette was a sickly, barely literate girl of fourteen when, in 1858, she saw eighteen apparitions of Our Lady in the grotto of Massabielle. The Lady called herself the Immaculate Conception. Questioned by civil and Church authorities, she held to her account. She entered the Sisters of Charity at Nevers in 1866 and died there, after long illness, in 1879.

people.name: St Joan of Arc
people.bio: A peasant girl of Domrémy, Joan believed that Saints Michael, Catherine and Margaret told her to relieve Orléans and have the Dauphin crowned at Reims. She led French troops in 1429 and was taken by the Burgundians the next year. Tried for heresy at Rouen by a court of pro-English clerics, she was burned on 30 May 1431. A retrial in 1456 declared the sentence void.

people.name: St Francis of Assisi
people.bio: The son of a wealthy cloth merchant of Assisi, Francis gave up his inheritance about 1206 to live in poverty and rebuild ruined churches. Companions gathered round him, and Innocent III approved his first rule orally in 1209. He preached to the poor, travelled to Egypt and the Holy Land, and received the stigmata at La Verna in 1224. He died at the Portiuncula on 3 October 1226.

people.name: St Clare of Assisi
people.bio: Born at Assisi into a noble family, Clare heard Francis preach and, on Palm Sunday 1212, left her father's house by night to receive the habit at the Portiuncula. She settled at San Damiano, where she gathered the community later called the Poor Clares. She ruled it as abbess for about forty years and fought to keep strict poverty. The pope confirmed her rule two days before she died in 1253.

people.name: St Vincent de Paul
people.bio: A Gascon peasant's son, Vincent was ordained in 1600 and, after a period of ambition, gave himself to the poor and to the clergy. He founded the Congregation of the Mission (Lazarists) in 1625 for country missions and the training of priests, and with Louise de Marillac the Daughters of Charity. His Confraternities of Charity, hospitals and relief of galley slaves served the poor of France until his death in Paris in 1660.

people.name: St Louise de Marillac
people.bio: Born in Paris in 1591, Louise de Marillac married Antoine Le Gras and bore a son. Widowed in 1625, she placed herself under the direction of Vincent de Paul and joined him in the work of the Confraternities of Charity among the sick poor. With him she founded the Sisters of Charity, who nursed the sick and taught poor children. She governed the community until her death in Paris on 15 March 1660, a few months before Vincent.

people.name: St Joseph of Cupertino
people.bio: Born in a stable at Cupertino in the Kingdom of Naples to a poor widow, Joseph was slow at his studies and was dismissed by the Capuchins. The Conventual Franciscans received him, and he was ordained priest in 1628. He became known for ecstasies in which he was said to rise from the ground. For decades he was kept apart from the community and moved between houses. He died at Osimo on 18 September 1663.

people.name: St Maria Goretti
people.bio: Maria Goretti was born at Corinaldo in 1890 to a farming family who later moved to the Pontine marshes near Nettuno. In July 1902, when she was eleven, a young neighbour, Alessandro Serenelli, tried to assault her; she refused and he stabbed her fourteen times. She died the next day, 6 July, after forgiving him. Serenelli repented in prison years later. She was beatified in 1947 and canonised in 1950.

people.name: St Thérèse of Lisieux
people.bio: Born at Alençon in 1873, Thérèse Martin was the youngest of nine children of devout parents. She asked Leo XIII's leave to enter the Carmel of Lisieux at fifteen and was admitted in April 1888. Her short religious life was hidden, marked by trust in God and small duties. She died of tuberculosis on 30 September 1897. Her autobiography, Story of a Soul, was published in 1898 and spread her fame quickly.

people.name: St Martin de Porres
people.bio: Born in Lima in 1579, the son of a Spanish nobleman and a freed Panamanian woman, Martin was apprenticed to a barber-surgeon. He entered the Dominican convent of the Rosary in Lima as a lay helper, and was admitted as a lay brother. There he nursed the sick, fed the poor and cared for stray animals, and was known for his humility. He died on 3 November 1639. He was beatified in 1837 and canonised in 1962.

people.bio: Born at Reims in 1651 into a wealthy family, La Salle became a canon and priest. Asked to help found schools for poor boys, he gave up his canonry and fortune and gathered teachers into the Brothers of the Christian Schools. He developed teaching in the vernacular and in classes, and set up training colleges for teachers. He died at Saint-Yon, near Rouen, on Good Friday, 7 April 1719.

people.name: St John Bosco
people.bio: Born to a poor peasant family at Becchi, near Turin, Bosco was ordained in 1841 and began to gather the young apprentices and street boys of the city on Sundays. He founded oratories, workshops and schools, and in 1859 the Salesian Society, followed by the Sisters of Mary Help of Christians. He placed his work under St Francis de Sales and relied on kindness rather than punishment. He died at Turin on 31 January 1888.

people.name: St Dominic Savio
people.bio: Born near Chieri in Piedmont in 1842, Dominic Savio came at twelve to Don Bosco's oratory in Turin, where he was known for his piety, his cheerfulness and his care for the other boys. He helped found a small sodality in honour of the Immaculate Conception. His health failed, and he died at Mondonio on 9 March 1857, aged fourteen. He was beatified in 1950 and canonised in 1954.

people.name: St Ignatius of Loyola
people.bio: A Basque nobleman and soldier, Ignatius was wounded at Pamplona in 1521 and, while recovering, read lives of Christ and the saints. After a year of prayer at Manresa he wrote the Spiritual Exercises. He studied at Paris, where he gathered companions, among them Francis Xavier. Paul III approved the Society of Jesus in 1540. He directed it from Rome as its first superior general until his death on 31 July 1556.

people.name: St Anthony Mary Claret
people.bio: Born at Sallent, near Barcelona, in 1807, Claret worked as a weaver before ordination in 1835. He preached popular missions through Catalonia and in 1849 founded the Missionary Sons of the Immaculate Heart of Mary (Claretians). As archbishop of Santiago de Cuba from 1851 he reformed the diocese and survived several attempts on his life. Recalled to Spain as confessor to Queen Isabella II, he died at Fontfroide in France in 1870.

people.name: St Thomas More
people.bio: Born in London in 1478, More was a lawyer, scholar and friend of Erasmus, the author of Utopia, and in 1529 became Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII. He resigned in 1532 when the king claimed headship of the Church in England. Refusing to swear the oath required by the Act of Succession, he was imprisoned in the Tower and, after trial for treason, beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535.

people.name: St Thomas Becket
people.bio: Born in London about 1118, Becket rose through the household of Archbishop Theobald to become Henry II's chancellor. Made archbishop of Canterbury in 1162, he defended the Church's rights against the king's Constitutions of Clarendon and spent six years in exile in France. Soon after returning, he was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral by four of the king's knights on 29 December 1170. Alexander III canonised him in 1173.

people.name: St Peter
people.bio: A Galilean fisherman of Bethsaida, Simon was called by Christ with his brother Andrew and given the name Peter. He confessed Jesus as the Christ at Caesarea Philippi and was named the rock on which the Church would be built, though he denied his Lord on the night of the Passion. He led the apostles after Pentecost, and tradition holds that he died at Rome under Nero.

people.name: St Paul
people.bio: Born Saul at Tarsus, a Pharisee and Roman citizen, Paul took part in persecuting the first Christians until Christ appeared to him on the road to Damascus. After his conversion he made three missionary journeys through Asia Minor and Greece, founded churches and wrote the letters that form part of the New Testament. Arrested at Jerusalem, he was taken to Rome, where tradition says he was beheaded under Nero.

Tradition adds that he lived to old age and was buried in Greece.

people.name: St Pius X
people.bio: Giuseppe Sarto was born at Riese in the Veneto in 1835, the son of a postman. Priest, bishop of Mantua and Patriarch of Venice, he was elected pope in 1903 and took as his motto to restore all things in Christ. He promoted frequent Communion and the early Communion of children, reformed sacred music and the Breviary, issued a catechism and condemned Modernism in 1907. He died on 20 August 1914, soon after the First World War began.

people.name: St Teresa of Ávila
people.bio: Born at Ávila in 1515, Teresa entered the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation at twenty and spent years in a lax community, suffering poor health and lapses in prayer. About 1560 she resolved on a stricter life and founded St Joseph's at Ávila in 1562, the first house of the Discalced Carmelites. She founded convents across Spain, with John of the Cross as her ally, and wrote the Life and The Interior Castle. She died at Alba de Tormes in 1582.

people.name: St John of the Cross
people.bio: Born John de Yepes at Fontiveros in 1542, he joined the Carmelites and, meeting Teresa of Ávila, helped her to extend her reform to the friars. Opposed by the unreformed brethren, he was imprisoned at Toledo in 1577 and escaped after nine months. He wrote the poems and treatises, The Ascent of Mount Carmel and The Dark Night, on the soul's path to union with God. He died at Úbeda on 14 December 1591.

people.name: St Rita of Cascia

After he was killed in a feud and her two sons died, she sought admission to the Augustinian convent at Cascia and was received after repeated refusals. She lived there as a nun, noted for penance and prayer. She died in 1457. Veneration of her, as patron of desperate cases, spread widely.

Ordained priest in 1551, he gathered young men for prayer, spiritual reading and works of charity, from which the Congregation of the Oratory grew. He was known for his cheerful, humorous manner and as a confessor. He died in Rome on 26 May 1595, and the Oratory was approved in 1575.

people.name: St Anthony of Padua

Illness sent him to Italy, where his learning and preaching were discovered by chance. He taught theology to the friars and preached against heresy in northern Italy and France. He died near Padua on 13 June 1231, and Gregory IX canonised him within a year.

people.name: St Joseph
people.bio: Joseph, a carpenter of Nazareth of the house of David, was betrothed to Mary. The Gospel of St Matthew tells that, finding her with child, he was told by an angel in a dream not to fear to take her as his wife. He took her and the Child to Egypt to escape Herod and then back to Nazareth. He is last mentioned when Jesus was twelve. Devotion to him grew greatly from the later Middle Ages.

people.name: Bl Andrew Kim Taegon
people.bio: Born in 1821 into a Korean Christian family of the nobility, Kim Taegon was baptised at fifteen and sent to the seminary at Macao by the French missionaries. He was ordained priest at Shanghai in 1845, the first Korean priest. Returning secretly, he tried to open a sea route for foreign missionaries and was arrested in 1846. He was beheaded near Seoul on 16 September 1846, aged twenty-five.

people.name: St Jean-Marie Vianney
people.bio: Born near Lyons in 1786, Vianney grew up through the Revolution and, with difficulty over his studies, was ordained in 1815. In 1818 he was sent to the small parish of Ars, where he rebuilt the spiritual life of the village by prayer, penance and sermons. From the 1830s pilgrims flocked to him, and he spent many hours daily in the confessional. He died at Ars on 4 August 1859.

people.name: St Catherine of Siena
people.bio: Born at Siena in 1347, the youngest of a large family of a dyer, Catherine became a Dominican tertiary while living at home. She served the sick and the poor, and gathered a circle of disciples. Her letters urged peace among the Italian states and pressed Gregory XI to return the papacy from Avignon, which he did in 1377. She worked for Urban VI during the Western Schism and died in Rome on 29 April 1380.

people.name: Bl John Houghton
people.bio: Born about 1487 in Essex and educated at Cambridge, Houghton was a parish priest before becoming a Carthusian. He was prior of the London Charterhouse from 1531. When Henry VIII required the oath acknowledging him as head of the English Church, he refused, and with other priors was arrested. Tried for treason, he was hanged, drawn and quartered at Tyburn on 4 May 1535, the first of the Carthusian martyrs.

people.name: St Paul Miki
people.bio: Born near Osaka about 1562 to a Japanese military family, Paul Miki was educated by the Jesuits and joined them. He was an eloquent preacher. When Hideyoshi began persecuting Christians, he was arrested with Franciscans and other Japanese Christians, and the group was marched to Nagasaki. They were crucified on a hill outside the city on 5 February 1597, and he preached from the cross.

Sent to Mexico for ordination, he sailed in 1596, but his ship was wrecked on the coast of Japan. He was arrested with other Christians at Kyoto and Osaka and marched to Nagasaki. He was crucified there on 5 February 1597, the first Mexican saint.

people.name: St Hildegard of Bingen
people.bio: Born in 1098 at Bermersheim in the Rhineland, Hildegard was given as a child to the Benedictine anchoress Jutta and became abbess of the community in 1136. From about 1141 she recorded her visions in the Scivias, and she later wrote on natural science and medicine, composed music and carried on a wide correspondence with popes, emperors and bishops. She founded Rupertsberg near Bingen, and died there on 17 September 1179.

people.name: St Augustine of Hippo
people.bio: Born at Tagaste in North Africa in 354 to a pagan father and the Christian Monica, Augustine taught rhetoric at Carthage, Rome and Milan and for years followed the Manichees. Moved by Ambrose's preaching and by his mother's prayers, he was baptised at Milan at Easter 387. He became bishop of Hippo in 396. His Confessions and The City of God, and his writings against the Donatists and Pelagians, shaped Western theology. He died in 430.

people.name: St Sebastian
people.bio: Sebastian was a Roman martyr buried on the Appian Way, where a basilica was built over his tomb about 367. His acts, written much later, say that he came from Milan, served as an officer in the imperial guard and secretly helped Christians. Condemned, he was shot with arrows, recovered, and was then beaten to death with clubs. He is invoked against plague. His cult is attested in Rome from the fourth century.

people.name: St Agnes

Her feast on 21 January is recorded in the Roman calendar of 354, and her tomb is on the Via Nomentana, where a basilica was built. Her name appears in the Canon of the Mass. The later Acts describe her refusing marriage to a pagan suitor and being put to death.

people.name: St Dismas
people.bio: Dismas is the name tradition gives to the repentant thief crucified at Christ's right hand. The Gospel of St Luke records that he rebuked his fellow criminal, acknowledged that he and his companion suffered justly, and asked Jesus to remember him in His kingdom. Christ promised him that he would be with Him that day in Paradise. The name Dismas appears in later apocryphal writings, and the thief has been honoured as a saint.

people.name: St Mary Magdalene

She stood at the foot of the Cross and was among the women who went to the tomb on Easter morning, where she was the first to see the risen Lord. In the West she was long identified with Mary of Bethany and with the penitent woman of Luke 7, an identification the Church's liturgy followed.

After he was murdered, she repented publicly and was received as a Franciscan tertiary at Cortona. She lived by penance, cared for the sick and poor and helped found a hospital. She died at Cortona on 22 February 1297.

She died at Lima on 24 August 1617, in her thirty-second year, the first saint of the Americas.

people.bio: Born in Roman Britain, Patrick was seized by raiders at about sixteen and taken to Ireland as a slave, where he herded sheep and turned to prayer. He escaped after six years, studied for the priesthood and later returned to Ireland as a bishop. He preached and baptised across the island, ordained clergy and founded churches. His own Confession and Letter to Coroticus survive. The traditional date of death is 17 March.

people.name: St Wenceslas
people.bio: Born near Prague and brought up as a Christian by his grandmother Ludmila, Wenceslas became duke of Bohemia in his teens. His brother Boleslav, who opposed his policy, invited him to a feast and had him murdered at Stará Boleslav on the way to Mass, probably on 28 September 935. He is patron of Bohemia.

people.bio: Barbara is an early virgin martyr whose Acts are legendary. They say her pagan father shut her in a tower and, when she became a Christian, handed her to the judge, then beheaded her himself. Her name is in the oldest martyrologies of the Latin Church, and her cult spread widely in the East and West. She is invoked against sudden death and is patroness of artillerymen and miners.

She lived a life of prayer and charity at court, founded hospitals and a convent, and more than once made peace between her husband and their son Afonso, and later between Afonso and the king of Castile. Widowed in 1325, she became a Franciscan tertiary. She died at Estremoz in 1336 while on a mission of peace.

people.name: Sts Cyril and Methodius
people.bio: Brothers from Thessalonica, Constantine (who took the name Cyril as a monk) and Methodius were sent from Constantinople to Great Moravia in 863 at Prince Rastislav's request. Cyril devised the Glagolitic script, and the two translated the Gospels and liturgical books into Slavonic. Frankish clergy opposed this, but Pope Hadrian II approved it. Cyril died in Rome in 869. Methodius, made archbishop of Moravia and Pannonia, was imprisoned by the Franks, later restored, and died in 885.

people.name: St Benedict of Nursia
people.bio: Born at Nursia about 480 and sent to study at Rome, Benedict withdrew to a cave near Subiaco and lived as a hermit. Disciples gathered round him, and he founded small monasteries nearby. About 530 he went to Monte Cassino, where he wrote the Rule that became the pattern of Western monasticism. Almost all that is known of his life comes from the second book of Gregory the Great's Dialogues. He died at Monte Cassino about 543. Allied bombing destroyed the abbey in February 1944.

people.name: St Stephen of Hungary
people.bio: Born about 975 as Vajk, son of the pagan Magyar prince Géza, he was baptised Stephen. He married Gisela of Bavaria in 995 and succeeded his father in 997. After defeating his rival Koppány he asked Pope Sylvester II for the royal title and was crowned king in 1001. He organised the Hungarian dioceses and founded Benedictine monasteries such as Pannonhalma. His son Emeric died in 1031. Stephen died on 15 August 1038 and was canonised with Emeric in 1083.

people.name: St Nicholas of Flüe
people.bio: Born in 1417 at Flüeli in Unterwalden, Nicholas was a farmer, soldier and magistrate, married, with ten children. In 1467, with his wife's consent, he left his family to live as a hermit in the Ranft gorge near Sachseln, where he was reported to live without food. Visitors came to him for counsel. His advice, carried to the Diet of Stans in 1481, helped to avert civil war among the Swiss cantons. He died on 21 March 1487.

people.name: St Margaret Mary Alacoque
people.bio: Born in 1647 at Lhautecour in Burgundy, Margaret Mary Alacoque entered the Visitation convent at Paray-le-Monial in 1671. From 1673 to 1675 she reported apparitions in which Christ showed her His Heart and asked for Communion on the first Friday of the month, the Holy Hour, and a feast of the Sacred Heart. Her superiors doubted her until her confessor, the Jesuit Claude de la Colombière, judged the visions genuine. She died on 17 October 1690.

people.name: St Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows
people.bio: Francesco Possenti was born at Assisi on 1 March 1838, the eleventh of thirteen children of a prosperous family. After several bereavements he entered the Passionists in 1856 and took the name Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows. He was known for exact observance of the Rule and for devotion to the Passion, the Eucharist and Our Lady's sorrows. He died of tuberculosis at Isola del Gran Sasso on 27 February 1862, aged twenty-three.

people.name: St James the Greater
people.bio: One of the Twelve, James was a Galilean fisherman, son of Zebedee and brother of John. With Peter and John he was present at the raising of Jairus's daughter, the Transfiguration and the agony in Gethsemane. Acts records that Herod Agrippa I had him put to the sword about AD 44. A later tradition says he preached in Spain and that his body lies at Compostela, though it is not attested before the ninth century.

people.name: St Francis Xavier
people.bio: Born in 1506 at the castle of Xavier in Navarre, Francis studied at the University of Paris, where he met Ignatius of Loyola. With Ignatius and others he took vows at Montmartre in 1534, the beginning of the Society of Jesus. Sent east at the request of the king of Portugal, he reached Goa in 1542, preached in India, Malacca and the Moluccas, and landed in Japan in 1549. He died on the island of Sancian, off China, on 2 December 1552.

people.name: St Dominic de Guzman
people.bio: Born about 1170 at Caleruega in Old Castile, Dominic became a canon of Osma. From about 1203 he preached to the Albigensians in southern France and in 1206 founded a convent at Prouille for women converted from heresy. He gathered preachers into a community, which Honorius III approved as the Order of Preachers in 1216. The order took the Rule of St Augustine and became mendicant in 1221. Dominic died at Bologna on 6 August 1221.

people.name: St Maxentia (Sainte Maxence)
people.bio: According to the traditional account, Maxentia was an Irish or Scottish virgin of the fifth century who fled to France to avoid marriage to a pagan chieftain and lived as a recluse by the Oise near Senlis, in the diocese of Beauvais. Her suitor tracked her down and beheaded her at the place now called Pont-Sainte-Maxence. Her relics are venerated there, and the town takes its name from her. The Book of Saints (1921) calls the particulars lost or uncertain.

people.name: St Cecilia
people.status: Venerated as a virgin martyr at Rome from the fourth century
people.bio: A Roman virgin and martyr, buried in the Catacomb of Callistus, whose feast was kept at Rome by the fourth century in the church named for her in Trastevere. Her Acts, a later pious romance, tell how she won her husband Valerian and his brother Tiburtius to the faith, both being martyred, and how she survived the heated bath and three blows of the sword, living three days before she died. She is the patroness of church music.
